newsitem.title: USA: Rubin plays down threat of Japan bond sales.
newsitem.headline: Rubin plays down threat of Japan bond sales.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Wednesday played down the threat of Japanese dumping of U.S. bonds, saying he did not expect such sales and voicing confidence the market could absorb them if they occurred.

"Our markets are so deep and so broad that even if there was enormous concerted selling by a foreign country -- I have no reason to think it would occur -- our markets could absorb it readily," Rubin told reporters.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto rocked U.S. financial markets on Monday when he seemed to suggest Japan might sell U.S. government bonds and buy gold if Washington did not cooperate with Tokyo to stabilise currency rates.
The markets recovered on Tuesday after Japanese officials denied that Tokyo had any plans to dump U.S. securities, but weakened anew on Wednesday amid rumours of bond sales by a foreign central bank.

Japan is the biggest foreign investor in U.S. Treasury bonds, with holdings of about $300 billion. If it suddenly chose to sell them off, analysts said U.S. long-term interest rates could skyrocket, damaging the U.S. economy.
Rubin acknowledged that financial markets might be briefly disrupted by concerted selling by a foreign government. But he argued that America's fate was in its own hands.

"As long as we are fiscally responsible, as long as we have a sound currency, as long as we pursue sensible and sound economic policies, this is a place where people are going to want to invest," Rubin said. "If large sellers develop for any set of reasons, there will also be large buyers."
He called U.S. economic conditions "very good" and said that they were likely to remain so, adding that markets over time reflect such fundamentals.
Japan's holdings of U.S. bonds have mounted steadily over the last decade as the country has used the dollars earned on exports to America to buy securities here.

The steep increase in foreign ownership of U.S. bonds in recent years -- foreigners now hold close to 35 percent of the Treasury securities outstanding -- in that sense is the mirror image of the continued rise in the U.S. trade deficit.
The trade deficit climbed nearly 9 percent last year, to close to $115 billion, its highest level since 1988.
However, Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said that the deficit now was less worrying than in the past.
That is partly because the United States is using the foreign capital to build factories and buy equipment, rather than to purchase consumer goods.
"That equipment is raising the productivity of American workers and is an important part of strong export performance," Summers said.
